records.name: City Square Ceremonial Gathering Space
records.artists: Lewis Wandin-Bursill (Wurundjeri artist), who developed the Woi-wurrung language and etched designs on the seating, drawing on the diamond motif of his ancestor William Barak; a Wurundjeri Elder (name not given) provided the manna gum leaf sketch

records.summary: A ceremonial gathering space within Melbourne's new City Square, co-designed by Greenshoot Consulting with Wurundjeri Elders. A central circular granite paved area has Woi-wurrung language set into the ground plane, a semi-circular granite seat etched with a diamond motif, and a rotating, lockable bronze Smoking Ceremony Dish on a stone plinth. Planting was selected in consultation with Wurundjeri Elders. The space supports formal ceremony and informal yarning.
records.why_it_matters: It shows how a ceremonial element can be added to an already resolved public realm while meeting operational constraints such as circulation, train station operations and smoke management. The lockable, rotating dish and the use of Elder-authored motifs are useful references for durable, culturally authored detailing.
records.description: The project is a ceremonial gathering place within Melbourne's new City Square, co-designed by Greenshoot Consulting with Wurundjeri Elders. It was commissioned after the square's design documentation was complete, so it had to fit into a resolved public realm. It sits centrally, keeps pedestrian movement and event flexibility, and needed endorsement from Traditional Owners, State Government, City of Melbourne and MTM. Early coordination dealt with circulation, train station operations and smoke management. The main element is a bronze Smoking Ceremony Dish on a granite plinth sourced from Country. The dish is rotating and lockable, balancing safety, durability and ceremonial expression. A manna gum leaf motif is embossed on the dish and etched into the plinth, taken from a sketch by a Wurundjeri Elder. A pattern inside the dish references the manna gum flower. Woi-wurrung language is set into a bespoke circular paving pattern that differs from the rest of the plaza. Semi-circular granite seating carries etched artwork by a Wurundjeri artist, drawing on William Barak's diamond motif. Planting was selected in consultation with Wurundjeri Elders, and interpretive signage supports public learning. The bronze is designed to patinate with use and touch. The space accommodates formal ceremony and informal yarning.

records.name: Celebrating Wurundjeri Women - Franklin Street Panels
records.location_text: Melbourne CBD, Melbourne VIC (exact street not confirmed)
records.architect: Hassell, Weston Williamson + Partners and Rogers Stirk Harbour + Partners (joint State Library Station design)
records.first_peoples_collaborators: Greenshoot Consulting (created the Wurundjeri women Elder imagery); Wurundjeri Woi-wurrung Elders, particularly Aunty Joy Murphy Wandin AO; Wurundjeri Woi Wurrung Cultural Heritage Aboriginal Corporation and Bunurong Land Council Aboriginal Corporation (artwork development, station-wide credit)
records.other_team: CYP Design and Construction Joint Venture: Bouygues Construction, John Holland, Lendlease (builder); Maynard Design Consultancy (line-wide design and wayfinding); Arup, Arcadis, WSP (engineering)
records.summary: A public art display in an inner Melbourne streetscape showing a large illuminated portrait panel of Aunty Annie Borate (as written on the panel), set into a concrete and metal service structure beside a heritage red brick building. The panel reads 'My name is Aunty Annie' with a line of First Peoples language and a green diamond pattern background. A small plaque beside it appears to be titled 'Celebrating Wurundjeri Women'. A group is gathered for a guided tour.
records.why_it_matters: It shows how a utilitarian piece of street infrastructure can carry a named First Peoples woman, language and pattern, making people visible in the city centre.
records.description: The photo shows a street corner in Melbourne's central city, with a red brick heritage building with cream rendered detailing on the left and high-rise towers behind. A concrete and metal structure topped by a ventilation stack has been fitted with a large framed display panel. The panel has a green background with a pale diamond pattern. It carries the text 'My name is Aunty Annie', a line in First Peoples language, and a black and white archival-style portrait of a woman. Smaller text curves around the portrait and includes 'Aunty Annie Borate' and 'I will be strong, I am strong'. A small plaque to the left of the panel appears to read 'Celebrating Wurundjeri Women', though it is hard to read in the photo. A group of people stands in front of the panel, apparently on a guided walk or tour, with a speaker facing them. The Instagram page text gave no caption, so designers, artists, date, client and Traditional Owner involvement are not confirmed from this material.

records.name: Ceremonial Fire Dish at Queen & Collins
records.location_text: Queen & Collins, 376-390 Collins Street, Melbourne VIC
records.architect: Greenaway Architects (fire dish design, with Greenshoot Consulting)
records.first_peoples_collaborators: Greenshoot Consulting (co-design); Wurundjeri Traditional Owners (engagement); Uncle Colin Hunter Jnr, Wurundjeri (co-designer of the fire dish)
records.awards: 2023 Good Design Award, Built Environment Installation Design
records.summary: A ceremonial fire dish installed in 2023 as part of the Queen & Collins redevelopment in Naarm/Melbourne. It was co-designed by Greenshoot Consulting through engagement with Wurundjeri Traditional Owners. Bronze etchings in the dish represent the topography and precolonial waterways of central Melbourne, and nearby significant First Peoples landmarks are shown in an embedded wayfinding device. The dish sits in a paved court with granite and bronze text inscriptions.
records.why_it_matters: It shows how a small, object-scale element in a commercial redevelopment can carry Country, waterways and landmarks through etched mapping and wayfinding. It also shows co-design with Traditional Owners producing an award-recognised outcome.
records.description: The ceremonial fire dish was originally installed in 2023 as part of the Queen & Collins redevelopment in Naarm/Melbourne. Greenshoot Consulting co-designed it through its engagement with Wurundjeri Traditional Owners. It won the 2023 Good Design Award for Built Environment Installation Design. The bronze etchings within the dish represent the topography and precolonial waterways of the centre of Naarm/Melbourne. Significant First Peoples landmarks close to the project site are also featured in the embedded wayfinding device. The project was again open to visitors as part of Open House Melbourne. The photo shows the bronze dish with etched contour and waterway lines, set beside a granite surface with bronze inscriptions including 'Site of first recorded Aboriginal burial' and a line referring to a place for reflection. Eucalyptus foliage and dark stones sit beside the dish, and brick paving surrounds the court. The second image is a render of the wider redevelopment, showing towers, a playing field and rooftop planting.
